subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Trial and Error in Games
description: A micro-lesson that makes Trial and Error in Games usable.

hook.text: A poker beginner bluffs randomly and loses. After 100 hands, she bluffs selectively and starts winning.

buildup.text: Reinforcement learning: repeat actions that worked, avoid actions that failed. No theory needed.

discovery.text: Erev and Roth showed reinforcement learning explains lab behavior better than Nash equilibrium in many simple repeated.

twist.text: Reinforcement learning can lock into bad strategies. If an early lucky win follows a bad play, the learner repeats.

climax.text: Early luck distorts learning. To improve, track why you won, not just that you won. Process matters more than outcome.

punchline.text: Winning by luck teaches nothing. Winning by process teaches everything.

quiz.question: What is the danger of reinforcement learning in games?
options: It always finds the optimal strategy quickly
It can lock into bad strategies if early luck reinforces poor choices
It requires reading complex strategy books

details.summary: Trial and error learning in games describes how players try different strategies, observe the outcomes, and gradually gravitate toward strategies that produced better results, without understanding why those strategies work.
details.whyItMatters: Most strategic learning in everyday life is trial and error rather than analytical reasoning. This model explains how people, firms, and organizations adapt strategies over time without formal game-theoretic knowledge.
takeaways: Players reinforce strategies that produced good outcomes previously
No understanding of the game structure or opponent reasoning is required
Reinforcement learning can converge to equilibrium but often very slowly

faq.question: Can simple trial and error reach optimal strategies?
faq.answer: Sometimes, but not always. In simple games with clear feedback, reinforcement learning converges to equilibrium. In complex games with delayed or noisy feedback, trial and error can get stuck in suboptimal patterns indefinitely.

faq.question: How does trial and error differ from belief-based learning?
faq.answer: Trial and error only strengthens strategies that were tried and worked. Belief-based learning also considers what would have worked for unchosen strategies. Trial and error requires no model of opponents; belief-based learning does.
